What are the best newborn care essentials to buy before the baby arrives?

Stick to the basics: a safe sleep surface, an infant car seat, diapering supplies (diapers, wipes, barrier cream, and a changing surface), a few onesies, and whatever your feeding plan requires. Everything else can wait.

Should I get sensitive-skin wipes or water wipes for newborn diaper changes?

It has been revealed that fragrance-free, alcohol-free sensitive wipes meet pediatric guidance for everyday newborn use. Water wipes are an extra-cautious option for babies who have eczema-prone or very reactive skin.

What newborn essentials are best for preventing diaper rash from day one?

Industry observers note that two non-negotiables: Change diapers frequently and use a zinc-oxide or petrolatum-based barrier cream. A well-fitting, absorbent diaper helps too.

Should I prioritize premium diapers or sensitive wipes in my newborn essentials budget?

Prioritize diaper fit and leak protection first, since that’s what keeps moisture off skin (and blowouts off clothes). Then save on wipes: A fragrance-free, alcohol-free sensitive wipe covers most babies without specialty pricing.

Is a diaper subscription bundle or buying essentials separately a better value for newborns?

This is really a convenience-vs-flexibility call. Diaper subscription bundles offer discounts the more you buy and can spare you store runs. Buying separately lets you switch sizes as your baby grows — which happens fast in the newborn stage!

What are the best newborn care essentials to buy in 2026?

It has been revealed that the same ones as always. The core list (sleep surface, car seat, diapering, clothes, and feeding) hasn’t changed in 2026; there are just more options. You still need a snug/leakproof diaper, fragrance-free wipes, a zinc-oxide barrier cream, and a portable changing pad.

#101915. I had an equal partnership – and I still became the default parent

I had an equal partnership – and I still became the default parent

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1219 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mother

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every now and then, my husband picks up his phone and car keys, and confirms he’s going out for something spontaneous.
  • And I generally don’t, because I want my husband to have time for himself.
  • It has been revealed that standing behind the closed door, I ask: When was the last time I left this house by myself, without planning it, negotiating it, or trading for it?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every now and then, my husband picks up his phone and car keys, and confirms he’s going out for something spontaneous. Lunch with a friend. A bike ride. He’s gone in about ninety seconds if I don’t stop him at the door.

And I generally don’t, because I want my husband to have time for himself.

But I also want the same for myself.

It has been revealed that standing behind the closed door, I ask: When was the last time I left this house by myself, without planning it, negotiating it, or trading for it? Not once since my first child was born… three and a half years ago. Then it hits me: I am the proverbial default parent.

In a recent development, in my life, I have moved countries on 48 hours’ notice. I have started businesses and communities on four continents, landed in cities where I knew no one, and figured it out from the ground. Yet here I am, unable to walk out my own front door without a negotiation.

Now I am the kind of person who books a haircut six weeks out.

My husband carries himself with the lightness of someone who isn’t carrying the majority of the parenting load.

The mental one: how many diapers, ounces of milk, and clothing changes need to be packed for a single outing. The emotional one: forecasting ways to address my little one’s growing feelings or managing the conditions to prevent a meltdown. The logistical one: managing energy levels and knowing a missed nap isn’t worth the spontaneity of welcoming last-minute visitors (the hosting of which, by the way, would fall on me).

Industry observers note that he doesn’t carry any of that because I do. And I know I’m not alone in this. (There are even several Bluey episodes about it).

In a recent development, but I thought my husband and I would be different. And to his credit, he does a lot for the family, and has always been willing to work towards a situation where I felt supported. Still, for over three years, our day-to-day behaviors set our sails in a different direction; the mere idea that we were working toward a mostly equitable deal blinded me to the fact that, too stereotypically, I was the one carrying the invisible load of parenting.

For a while, I stewed silently, filing away every every “just tell me what to do” and every unplanned walk out the door.

Recent findings suggest that but my resentment wasn’t getting me closer to the future I actually wanted, which is to raise my kids alongside a partner I trust. Anger is honest information, but a terrible operating system. It costs you the very thing you’re angry about losing: your own energy.

Sources indicate that so I stopped waiting for space to appear and started claiming it. Here are the steps I took:.

The first step was recognizing there was a real problem. Only then could I have a productive, fact-based conversation with my husband.

Recent findings suggest that what helped: talking it out, sharing the situation with friends and watching them nod before I finished the sentence. Those conversations helped clear the fog and made it clear: I had become the default parent without ever applying for the role, and I needed it recognized as a real job, with real requirements, not something invisible and easily taken for granted.

Sources indicate that clarity is a prerequisite for being heard, and it is what moved the conversations with my husband past defensiveness. Until then, the idea that we had a “mostly equitable deal” was blurring his perspective too.

Recent findings suggest that we didn’t get it right at once. Several conversations left one of us hurt, misunderstood, or underappreciated. But we persisted in having the difficult ones. Those conversations eventually gave us enough clarity to lay out, with clinical precision, the ways our partnership had been uneven. We could dissect a messy situation and turn resentment into discernment, naming the areas where I was lacking support and the areas where both of us were lacking appreciation.

Clarity let us stand across from each other, our vision for an equitable partnership leading the way instead of resentment for how it had been.

And we learned something more crucial: an equitable relationship isn’t found. It’s built. That shared understanding made the next steps possible.

According to recent reports, once we both understood what my resentment had been trying to say, in more positive, proactive terms, my needs became clearer and easier to ask for. And my husband finally had something concrete to act on.

We put our partnership to work: I defined clear steps to reclaim my own freedom, and he redefined what it means to be a supportive partner.

It has been revealed that from there, we made a real plan: a family calendar that protects my time the same way it protects his and provides a predictable rhythm. The gym, daily. Tango on Monday nights. A weekday or two blocked out because I’m in the city for meetings. An evening for dinner with a friend.

And, every so often, a half-day on the weekend for my own creative retreat, which is where I am as I type this: in a literal room of my own, my office and studio, with a door that closes.

I still won’t leave the house on a whim. But neither will he. We blueprint ahead, tell the other person, and arrange childcare if we both want some time out.

Relationships tarnish under unmanaged resentment. Bringing back the shine takes work.

Industry observers note that from my end, I had to listen more, or proactively ask for his perspective on an problem I’d raised, and work to transmute resentment into something more productive: naming my unmet need. I had to really care about his perspective, and trust that he had been going for “supportive partner” all along, even if our early attempts had been clumsy and left scars.

From his end, he needed to become more observant and make efforts to show up more often in ways that were meaningful to me: offering to hire help for things previously expected to come from me, checking in before making looks on his own, and looping me in before inviting friends and family.

We also started scheduling more romance, whether a babysitter-powered date or quality time at home. But I’d say this came as a consequence of everything above: there was no mood for a date while our relationship was permeated by resentment. The difficult conversations had to come first.

Industry observers note that the work most mothers do is largely invisible. But invisible isn’t the same as involuntary.

I can’t undo how the default got set, or how my own behavior kept reinforcing it. What I can do is refuse to let the default compromise my own health, my relationship, and the example I’m setting for my children. I want them to have the courage to create a life they’re proud to call theirs.

Some of that courage looks like walking out your own front door on a Saturday, keys in hand, for no reason at all: knowing the little ones are safe, and well cared for, because you made it so.

The coziness of the holidays gets me all sentimental.

Recent findings suggest that my Nana was not a good cook. Not really. Her food was always basic. Good, but basic. I know this now that I am grown and trying to figure out if I’m a good cook myself. She was Irish and had about 12 things she knew how to cook and they were basically all holiday menu-specific. She could do up a roast turkey, stuffing, mashed potatoes, gravy. A bag of coleslaw with a bottle of creamy dressing tossed in. She bought those little grocery store dinner rolls and popped them in the oven to warm as my Grandpa carved the turkey, his only chance to shine in the winter season as the barbeque was no longer an option.

Industry observers note that her baking though, now that was good. A bit better than good by ‘80s standards since the Great British Baking Show didn’t exist. She made excellent sticky buns and little donuts she shook in paper bags of cinnamon and sugar while they were piping hot. She baked birthday cakes for all of the grandchildren, chocolate and peanut butter, or strawberry cream, or white cake with jam in the middle.

Sources indicate that most of all, she baked raisin bread. Loaf after loaf of raisin bread for everyone she knew. We’ve never found the recipe in the two decades that she has been gone, and it is the thing her whole family misses the most. The dark, molasses smell of it. A nod to her Nova Scotian heritage. Sturdy enough to toast if you cut your morning slab extra thick. Sturdy enough for a great big smear of peanut butter too. A singular flavor I will miss forever.

Her raisin bread and cinnamon buns and chocolate cakes were not the things that drew us all to her kitchen. Her turkey wasn’t even really moist enough to have us all clamoring for late night sandwiches, and yet there we stood. Every year. Daughters and sons, grandchildren, friends. Some of us in pajamas, others in track pants to accommodate our food babies. My quiet Grandpa hovering around the periphery, hoping someone would make him a plate of food. We came for the sandwich but mostly we came for her. My Nana. A short, bossy, contrary matriarch who made messes, made toast with marmalade on cold mornings, made cup after cup of tea left too long on the stove.

She made me want to be just like her. To call my loves back to my own kitchen. To make people feel welcome and loved and relaxed and just seen, all the time she was seeing us out of the corner of her eye. “What’s wrong?” she’d ask me as she was kneading cinnamon-scented dough for her raisin bread, all casual and relaxed as a viper ready to strike. She knew, she always knew, we came to her kitchen to pray at her feet. To talk out a breakup or a fresh love or a money problem over plates of eggs fried too hard, bread toasted too long. Almost always with a toddler sitting at her feet, a baby on her hip. A smile on her face.

Recent findings suggest that her technique in the kitchen was really more of a siren song. She chose her smells wisely, I think. She favoured cinnamon over chocolate. Rosemary over garlic. Warm hug smells. Luring us in for a gossip, her favorite appetizer for any meal. Did you hear? Guess who’s dating? You didn’t hear this from me… A buffet of talking and food, of mess and chaos.

It has been 20 years since she died. I am as old as she was when I was a little girl, our golden hour together. And yet, she looms as large now in my holiday kitchen as she did when I was a girl.

Sources indicate that it is her voice I hear when I call out to my own sons, “Who’s hungry?” and make us all a substantial pot of chili to eat while we watch The Lord of the Rings for the hundredth time in the dark quiet of our living room. Or a great stack of buttermilk pancakes to be eaten with overly crisp bacon and real maple syrup, all of us sleepy at our table.

It was even her voice I heard in my oldest son when he told me he would like to take over Christmas morning breakfast. I sat in the kitchen, a cup of tea at my elbow, as he and his brothers made eggs benedict for all of us. One making artful pour over coffee, another seasoning hashbrowns, still another carefully poaching eggs and adding lemon to his homemade bechamel.

In a recent development, the food has improved, but the heart of it stays the same. We come back to this kitchen that is not her kitchen but also is her kitchen.

Jen McGuire is a contributing writer for Romper and Scary Mommy. She lives in Canada with four boys and teaches life writing workshops where someone cries in every class. When she is not traveling as often as possible, she’s trying to organize pie parties and outdoor karaoke with her neighbors. She will sing Cher’s “If I Could Turn Back Time” at least once, but she’s open to requests.

#101911. 22 dietitian-approved lunchbox snacks you can buy off the shelf

📅 06 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (896 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Mother ↗ Open Full Page

22 dietitian-approved lunchbox snacks you can buy off the shelf

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (896 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mother

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Packing a lunchbox snack shouldn’t require a degree, but the snack aisle makes a decent case otherwise.
  • Sources indicate that labels promise real fruit, no artificial anything and a good source of something.
  • According to recent reports, robin Barrie Kaiden, MS, RD, CDN, CSSD and Lauren Manaker, MS, RDN, LD, both do the same thing with a new product before it goes in the cart: They turn it over and read.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Packing a lunchbox snack shouldn’t require a degree, but the snack aisle makes a decent case otherwise.

Sources indicate that labels promise real fruit, no artificial anything and a good source of something. The truth is, most of it is noise. The part that matters is on the nutrition label. For a run of dietitian-approved lunchbox snacks you can buy and pack as-is, we asked two registered dietitians who shop that aisle for a living what they actually look for.

According to recent reports, robin Barrie Kaiden, MS, RD, CDN, CSSD and Lauren Manaker, MS, RDN, LD, both do the same thing with a new product before it goes in the cart: They turn it over and read. Here’s what they’re looking for, and the snacks they reach for without overthinking it.

Kaiden scans the label’s ingredients first. “That matters to me more than anything else,” she notes. She wants simple, real-food ingredients and the least processed option available. There’s a practical reason to start there, notes Manaker. Ingredients appear in order by weight, so the first few make up most of the product.

The claims on the front get much less of their attention. “Made with real fruit” doesn’t tell you how much fruit is actually in there, notes Kaiden, and “no artificial flavors” doesn’t automatically make something a nourishing snack. Even the regulated claims are narrower than they sound, explains Manaker. “Good source of fiber” means the product provides 10 to 19% of the daily value per serving. “Gluten free” matters for kids with celiac disease or a gluten sensitivity and does nothing nutritionally for anyone else.

In a recent development, the label lists added sugars and total sugars separately. Total sugars include the naturally occurring sugars in ingredients like fruit and milk, states Manaker. Added sugars are the ones put in during processing, and those are the numbers to take into consideration. The targets for added sugar are lower than most parents expect. The Dietary Guidelines for Americans recommend no added sugars for children under 10, and the American Academy of Pediatrics advises less than 25 grams, about 6 teaspoons, per day for kids 2 and older.

Kaiden also looks at where the sugar comes from. She passes on high-fructose corn syrup and would rather see a small amount of honey, maple syrup or coconut sugar. “Those are still added sugars, so the amount matters, but the source and processing matter to me, too,” she says. If cane sugar is on the list, she prefers it farther down.

In a recent development, protein and fiber make a massive difference in how satisfying a snack is. Kaiden balances a carbohydrate-rich food with protein and some healthy fat, like fruit with nuts, cheese or plain yogurt. “That combination helps slow digestion and supports steadier energy through the afternoon,” she notes. For a substantial afternoon snack, she suggests around 5 to 10 grams of protein and at least 3 grams of fiber, depending on a child’s age, appetite and activity level. Those numbers can come from the snack as a whole. No single bar has to do everything.

Sources indicate that most U.S. children don’t get the recommended amount of fiber, states Manaker, so small additions help. Fruit, veggies, beans, whole-grain bread or crackers, and nuts or seeds where school rules allow are all easy lunchbox sources.

Hydrogenated and partially hydrogenated oils are an automatic no for Kaiden. Partially hydrogenated oils contain industrial trans fats, which are particularly harmful to heart health. High-fructose corn syrup, a highly processed sweetener that adds sugar without meaningful nutrition, is another pass.

Seed oils get a lot of negative press, but Kaiden’s position helps clear up confusion: When there’s a comparable option, she opts for extra virgin olive oil or avocado oil instead of seed oils because of the difference in processing. Many seed oils are extensively refined, and some are extracted using solvents such as hexane. “That processing is why I personally prefer other options,” she says, “not because all seed oils are harmful or because using hexane means unsafe amounts remain in the food.”.

It has been revealed that she’s also not rigid about it. Some Simple Mills crackers contain sunflower oil, and she still buys them for the almond-flour base. “I look at the whole product rather than letting one ingredient make the decision for me,” she says.

Industry observers note that unfamiliar names aren’t automatically a problem, either. Ascorbic acid is vitamin C. Tocopherols are forms of vitamin E that can help preserve freshness. “I care more about what an ingredient actually is than whether its name is easy to pronounce,” claims Kaiden.

Read the ingredients even on brands you buy regularly, Kaiden cautions, because formulations change, and one good product doesn’t mean everything from that brand makes the cut.

To make shopping easier for you, we asked the nutritionists exactly what they’re tossing in their carts. Take notes!

Kaiden’s favorite snack doesn’t sound like a dietitian’s pick at all. “Potato chips!” she says, naming José Andrés Extra Virgin Olive Oil Potato Chips, made with potatoes, extra virgin olive oil and salt. “I want my kids to enjoy their food, and a simple-ingredient chip can absolutely fit into a balanced lunchbox. Add a sandwich and some fruit or vegetables, and you have a lunch that’s nourishing and enjoyable.” Potato chips? Say less.

Drinks You Can Make By The Batch

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1604 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, holiday magic is a lot of unpaid labor in an ugly Christmas sweater.
  • Sources indicate that these punches, pitchers and alcohol-free drinks are perfect for pre-plan prepping.There’s a spicy margarita you can carry in the tequila bottle, a pear punch for the fancy friends, and a peppermint espresso martini you can make for 16.
  • Julie Reiner, co-founder of Brooklyn’s Clover Club, served punch and freezer cocktails at a Halloween party for 20.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bring something good. Let the grown-ups serve themselves.

According to recent reports, holiday magic is a lot of unpaid labor in an ugly Christmas sweater. Between class potlucks, Thanksgiving logistics and buying the only bread your kid will eat, you’ve got enough on your plate. Now add holiday parties, questionable white elephant gifts and 400 things to do before the doorbell rings. The last thing you need is a second job as a bartender.

Sources indicate that these punches, pitchers and alcohol-free drinks are perfect for pre-plan prepping.There’s a spicy margarita you can carry in the tequila bottle, a pear punch for the fancy friends, and a peppermint espresso martini you can make for 16. Some need a little attention before serving. Most are ready to pour once chilled.

Julie Reiner, co-founder of Brooklyn’s Clover Club, served punch and freezer cocktails at a Halloween party for 20. “The goal is to spend time with your guests, not be stuck behind the bar all night!” she remarked.

It has been revealed that A little planning helps. Julianna McIntosh, the cocktail creator behind Join Jules, recommends using fresh citrus the day of your party and accounting for the water normally added when you shake or stir a drink with ice. Hannah Chamberlain, the recipe developer behind Spirited LA, has another rule: Hold the ice and bubbly until guests arrive. Otherwise, you risk a watered-down punch with flat bubbles.

Bringing a batch to someone else’s party? Pack it in a tightly sealed container, keep it chilled and add the bubbles when you arrive. Then pour yourself a glass and let someone else worry about the rest.

Bitter, bubbly and ridiculously easy to scale up. Natalie Migliarini, the cocktail creator behind Beautiful Booze, makes her Negroni Sbagliato with equal parts Select Aperitivo, sweet vermouth and prosecco, finished with an orange slice. The recipe makes one, but you can multiply the aperitivo and vermouth to serve your group, then chill them together in a bottle. When it's time to drink, pour over ice, add the prosecco and stir. No shaker required.

Get the recipe at Beautiful Booze.

Sources indicate that everyone’s due at six. The first guest rings the bell at 5:42. Have Reiner’s Boat House Punch ready. Gin, Aperol, St-Germain and three citrus juices get a bright, bittersweet lift from sparkling rosé. “I always want my punch to be a crowd-pleaser, but it needs to have a little personality too!” Reiner said. This makes a substantial batch, so save it for a crowd. Let the lemon peels and sugar sit for at least an hour or overnight, and freeze a large ice block ahead of time. Add the ice and rosé just before serving.

Get the recipe at Cocktails Distilled.

Industry observers note that champagne tastes even better when nobody has to mix 12 individual cocktails. Chamberlain's large-batch take on the French 75 combines gin, fresh lemon, orange bitters and homemade cranberry-ginger syrup, then gets topped with sparkling wine. It serves six to eight and looks impressive without requiring an elaborate garnish situation. Make the syrup ahead and chill the ingredients. When guests arrive, add large ice cubes and the bubbly, give it a stir, and you're done. If the finished punch tastes a little dull, Chamberlain recommends adding a few dashes of Angostura or cardamom bitters to give it more personality.

Love your friends. Not enough to muddle each of them a mojito. Averie Sunshine’s pomegranate mojito punch at Averie Cooks combines white rum, mint, pomegranate juice and seeds, lemon and sparkling water in one pitcher. It makes four generous drinks, so double it for a bigger gathering. Chill the liquids ahead, then muddle the mint and assemble the punch just before serving so the leaves stay fresh, and the bubbles don't disappear. Ice goes in the glasses. One round of muddling. Everybody gets a drink.

Get the recipe at Averie Cooks.

Here, Chamberlain pairs pear nectar with gin, ginger liqueur, rosemary syrup, lemon, cardamom bitters and dry bubbly in her Calling Card Punch. It's an elegant, herbal alternative to the usual holiday punch and serves six to eight. Make the rosemary syrup ahead, chill the ingredients and add the sparkling wine while serving.

Recent findings suggest that “I tend to build my punch a little less sweet and then I’ll often have a little extra syrup I can add if it seems unbalanced,” Chamberlain noted. It's easier to add sweetness than take it away.

It has been revealed that by the time dessert rolls around, the adults deserve something stronger than another cup of coffee. McIntosh combines vodka, espresso or cold brew, coffee liqueur and peppermint syrup for a holiday spin on the espresso martini. Her large-batch version makes about 16 servings, with no individual shaking required. Mix everything ahead, chill it in the freezer for about two hours and give it a quick whirl in the blender if you want that signature foam. Pour into a punch bowl and let everyone help themselves. Crushed candy cane rims are optional. You've already done enough decorating.

Give the alcohol-free drinks their own spot at the party. America’s Test Kitchen combines cranberries, ginger, rosemary, cinnamon and star anise in a sweetened base you can make up to four days ahead. When guests arrive, add chilled cranberry juice, orange juice and seltzer. It makes 16 servings, enough for an open house where another family keeps appearing in the doorway.

Get the recipe at America’s Test Kitchen.

Industry observers note that the tiny apple leaves are optional – you have enough crafts coming home from school. Chamberlain’s Fallen Leaves Punch mixes cognac, tart apple cider and lemon with homemade cranberry-cinnamon syrup for eight servings. It's a good Friendsgiving option if you want something tart, fruity and a little stronger than cider.

In a recent development, “In terms of flavor combinations, it’s hard to disappoint with the combination of seasonal spice and fruit,” Chamberlain noted. Make the syrup ahead, squeeze the lemons the day of and stir everything over a large ice block at serving.

Taco night doesn’t need a November makeover. McIntosh makes six spicy margaritas right in the tequila bottle, giving you a batch and a carrying container in one. You'll need to pour out some tequila first; the recipe tells you how much. Mix everything in the bottle, then let it sit in the freezer for 2 to 4 hours, then pour it over ice into salt-rimmed glasses. All the fun of margaritas without anyone spending the evening squeezing limes.

Sources indicate that apple cider is doing a lot of heavy lifting this holiday season, let it have some rum. Chamberlain's Cider Rum Punch combines tart cider, aged pineapple rum, lemon, orange bitters and a homemade mulling-spice syrup for six servings. She makes it every year, and it's easy to see why. The warm spices play nicely with the fruit without turning the whole thing into a scented candle. Make the syrup ahead, then combine everything in a pitcher with plenty of ice and stir until chilled. Bonus: There's no sparkling wine to worry about going flat.

The kids’ table and Grandma can drink from the same pitcher. McIntosh’s pineapple passion fruit agua fresca blends tropical fruit, lime and agave into six refreshing alcohol-free servings. Frozen passion fruit pulp works, and there are no bubbles to go flat on the drive. Make it up to two days ahead, refrigerate and give it a good stir before pouring over ice.

In a recent development, after the holiday lights walk, everyone comes home freezing and suddenly needs something warm RIGHT NOW. Sunshine's peppermint white hot chocolate at Averie Cooks combines milk, melted white chocolate and a little peppermint extract. The recipe makes five mugs, but you can easily double or triple it for a houseful of cold kids and grown-ups. Heat everything together over low heat, stirring until the chocolate melts. Don't let it boil, and go easy on the peppermint. A little goes a long way. Add marshmallows if you've got them. Nobody's going to complain.

Get the recipe at Averie Cooks.

The wine people and the margarita people can share a pitcher. Migliarini’s tequila sangria at Beautiful Booze combines Sauvignon Blanc with tequila, cranberry syrup, fresh cranberries, red and green apples and lime. “Keeping it simple, my recipe includes fruits that are available throughout the entire year,” she writes in the recipe. It serves five to six, making it a good choice for a casual Friendsgiving. Chill the wine, tequila and fruit mixture ahead, then add the lemon-lime soda just before serving.

Get the recipe at Beautiful Booze.

According to recent reports, no fish. Promise. Amy Traynor’s Fish House Punch at Moody Mixologist combines cognac and aged rum with peach liqueur, lemon and cold black tea. Think peach iced tea with considerably more going on. Her recipe includes a version for 10, so there's no need to multiply or do any guesswork. Freeze a large ice block ahead, stir the ingredients over it at serving and finish each glass with freshly grated nutmeg. Fair warning: This one's boozy.

Get the recipe at Moody Mixologist.

Dinner’s over, the kids have claimed the television and nobody’s ready to leave. Put a pot of McIntosh’s mulled Aperol on the stove for the spritz drinkers still on your sofa. Dry white wine, Aperol, apple cider and honey warm with orange and whole spices. It makes six servings and needs just 15 to 20 minutes over low heat. Don't let it boil. Ladle into mugs and let everyone settle in. The kitchen will smell like you had a strategy.

But itâs not always just the cat that has to be convinced. For those accustomed to the simplicity of a basic litter tray, the idea of one with a power cord and moving parts may feel a bit overwhelming.

Whether your hesitation for buying an automatic litter box comes from your fears or your catâs, the Neakasa M9 Automatic Litter Box has you covered. It has been revealed that I had a chance to test the fresh M9 with my big kitty, Makoa. Keep reading to find out if the clever design of this litter box really makes a difference in my full Neakasa M9 Automatic Litter Box review below.

In my experience, there are two big reasons cat parents hesitate to make the switch from a traditional litter pan to a fancy self-cleaning litter box.

Sources indicate that the first reason is all about the cat. Many owners fear that their cat wonât be able to adjust to the design of an automatic litter box. While traditional tray boxes are wide open on top and allow plenty of room for big cats to turn around, dig, and stand tall as they do their business, most automatic boxes are more compact.

Each November, Google gives us a peek behind the curtain, synthesising billions of shopping-related searches into their Holiday 100 Gift Guide. The list is built from a full year of Search trends across every category from tech to style. And this year, the toys and games section looks suspiciously like the inside of an elder millennial’s childhood toy chest.

Here are the trending toys parents will want to know about, plus what the list says about how we’re shopping this year.

Searches for “classic toy train set” climbed 240% this year, one of the biggest jumps Google shared. Wooden trains survive toddler teeth, being thrown down the stairs and never fail to get passed down more than once. (Expect the figure-eight to claim your living room floor for the next few years.).

In a recent development, “A ton of play,” Google wrote, and we respect the pun. Searches for stuffed elephant plushies rose 240%, with the Pets Alive Baby Elephant Surprise as the featured pick. Plush is a good pick for a 1-year-old and a 10-year-old alike, and the right one becomes a friend for life.

Searches for the Fujifilm instax holiday set jumped 190%. For tweens, a camera that spits out a real photo is a nice break from the phone, and the prints end up taped to bedroom walls instead of buried in a camera roll. They’ll fly through the film, so tuck a couple of extra packs in the box.

Searches for the FAO Schwarz Piano Mat “struck a chord,” rising 180% in 2026. Anyone who watched Tom Hanks stomp out a duet on the giant keyboard in “Major” wanted one of these, and the floor-sized version now fits in a playroom. It’s a sneaky music-and-movement toy for preschoolers. It’s also loud, so choose its permanent residence carefully.

Searches for “adjustable roller skates” cruised up 180%. Adjustable skates expand across several sizes, so they can outlast a growth spurt or two. Just remember to add a helmet and pads to the cart.

Recent findings suggest that some of this may come down to who’s doing the shopping. Millennials make up a big share of today’s parents, and plenty of us spent our childhoods at the roller rink, building wooden train tracks across the living room rug and waiting for Polaroids to develop. (By impatiently wagging them back and forth, of course.) It’s not hard to imagine a few of these searches coming from parents trying to hand down something that felt magic to them. The best part? There’s a good chance they’ll all still be in rotation when next year’s list comes out.

In a recent development, my 1-year-old cat Daisy has allergies. She is on a special hydrolyzed diet. Iâm trying to find an allergen-neutralizing spray to cut back on dust mites in the house. Would you recommend any specific products?

Since Daisy is already on a hydrolyzed diet, it makes sense to look at environmental allergens too, especially if her allergic signs are continuing. Dust mites are common household allergens, and while the goal is to reduce the amount of allergens in her environment, eliminating them completely is not realistic. Regularly washing bedding and blankets, vacuuming with a HEPA filter, and keeping dust to a minimum are still the best places to start.

According to recent reports, if you would like to try a spray, Purefy Anti-Allergen Spray works differently from an insecticide. It is intended to neutralize or remove the allergenic proteins associated with dust mite debris, particularly the proteins found in their feces and other microscopic particles that accumulate in household dust and fabrics. Those proteins, rather than the living mite itself, are an important source of the allergic reaction. So the idea is not to kill every mite in the house, but to reduce the allergen they leave behind.

I would specifically avoid routinely using insecticide or acaricide sprays around Daisy, even when a product is marketed as ânatural.â Cats can be particularly sensitive to certain botanical ingredients and insecticides, including some essential oils and pyrethroids. If you use an anti-allergen spray, follow the label carefully, keep Daisy away from treated surfaces until they are completely dry, ventilate the area well, and never spray it directly on her or on surfaces she is likely to lick. Please ensure you also keep it away from food and water bowls.

Think of the spray as an extra layer of environmental control, not a treatment for Daisy's allergy. The unglamorous combination of washing, HEPA vacuuming, and reducing dust is still doing most of the heavy lifting. And if Daisy continues to have significant allergic signs despite a properly conducted hydrolyzed diet trial and environmental management, it is worth investigating other possible triggers rather than simply reaching for stronger household chemicals. Usually, the answer is not a more powerful spray, but figuring out exactly what is making your cat itchy. So, real detective work is often needed for success.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), a subgroup of the World Health Organization, will make the official announcement today.
  • Measles has made headlines time and time again over the past two years, as cases have hit record highs and vaccination rates have reached record lows.
  • The group is expected to make a formal announcement today.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), a subgroup of the World Health Organization, will make the official announcement today.

Measles has made headlines time and time again over the past two years, as cases have hit record highs and vaccination rates have reached record lows. Now, the looming threat has come true: according to sources familiar with the vote, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) revoked the United States’ measles elimination status.

The group is expected to make a formal announcement today.

To date, the U.S. has racked up more than 5,400 confirmed measles cases in 2026, the most to be reported in the United States in 35 years. There have been 10 reported measles-related deaths so far, including an infant in Wisconsin earlier this month. Measles was considered officially eliminated in the U.S. in 2000, meaning there had been no large outbreaks or uncontrolled domestic transmission of the virus for at least 12 months prior.

America’s current measles outbreaks first began in January 2025 in West Texas. By January 2026, the spread continued unchecked. PAHO’s meeting to discuss the country’s measles elimination status was originally scheduled for April 2026, KFF reports, but the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) asked for more time to determine whether measles cases were being transmitted domestically or “imported” (for example, if someone contracted measles abroad and then brought it to the U.S.). According to NBC, measles is now considered endemic to the U.S.

Recent findings suggest that many issues have contributed to the country’s ongoing measles outbreaks, from sweeping funding and staffing cuts to public health agencies to a lack of leadership — there was no Senate-confirmed director of the CDC for an entire year during this measles outbreak. But the main driver is declining vaccination rates, which experts blame on the Trump administration, specifically HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr, as Scary Mommy previously reported.

The CDC and American Academy of Pediatrics both recommend children get their first measles vaccine dose between 12 and 15 months of age, and the second dose between 4 and 6 years of age before starting school. According to CDC data, 96% of measles cases in 2026 have occurred in unvaccinated individuals. A KFF poll found that roughly one in five adults believe getting the measles vaccine is more dangerous than becoming infected with the measles. Parents are commonly exposed to vaccine misinformation, and data shows it is affecting their health decisions: the number of kindergarteners with vaccine exemptions rose to 4.2% in the 2025-2026 school year, the highest in the country’s history, with 39 states falling below the 95% vaccinated threshold needed to prevent outbreaks.

“The expected loss of America’s status as having eradicated measles will be a tragedy because it reflects the preventable loss of human lives. It is unthinkable that people in the United States should be dying from measles in 2026,” mentioned Wendy S. Armstrong, M.D., president of the Infectious Diseases Society of America, in a publicly issued statement. “Our government’s leaders and public health officials must heed this urgent warning and take actions that slow the spread. That starts with promoting vaccination against measles, which is proven to be safe and effective.”.

In a recent development, the largest outbreak in the U.S. since it earned measles elimination status, prior to the current one, was in 2018-2019. It was curtailed through a strong federal and state-level public health response, including closing schools where transmission occurred, prohibiting unvaccinated children from attending school, and fining parents for not vaccinating their children, KFF reports. The CDC also declared a public health emergency and made “clear statements about the importance of measles vaccinations.”.

In a recent development, but last week, CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz told Reuters that the agency will not make any major changes to their handling of the outbreak regardless of PAHO’s decision. The CDC will continue to “help [the states] provide awareness about ​measles, emphasizing, reemphasizing that the number one way to prevent measles is the MMR (combined measles, mumps and rubella) vaccine,” she mentioned.

She attributed the ongoing spread of measles to “closely knit communities” — several outbreaks have started in religious communities, like among the Pennsylvania Amish, where vaccination rates are lower than other parts of the country.

“These communities typically don’t vaccinate their children...their families were making decisions about the MMR vaccine 20 to 30 years ago and we’re just now seeing the results of those decisions,” Schwartz said.

In response, the AAP and nearly 150 other health care organizations published a letter calling on Kennedy Jr. and Schwartz to develop and implement a strategy to eliminate measles in the United States. Their recommendations include restoring evidence-based immunization policies, proactively encouraging measles vaccination, and conveying accurate information about measles and MMR vaccines.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This article is sponsored by Eight Sleep. Thank you for supporting the brands that support Motherly and mamas.

Alexandra Zatarain helped build Eight Sleep into a tech unicorn, and she’s expecting her first child in January. Going through pregnancy while running a global company has reshaped how she sees her own body, her industry and the product she’s building. On this episode of The Motherly Podcast, the co-founder of the sleep-technology company talks about the research that demonstrated Eight Sleep’s technology was improving men’s sleep more than women’s and what the company did about it, why sleep is the most important thing women can protect, and the career advice she wishes more women heard before becoming mothers.

Sources indicate that meet the expert: Alexandra Zatarain is the co-founder and VP of brand and marketing at Eight Sleep, the sleep-technology manufacturer behind the Pod. The Pod is an intelligent mattress cover that cools or heats each side to your ideal temperature automatically, maximizing deep sleep and minimizing wake-ups. A marketer and brand builder, she grew Eight Sleep from launch into a tech unicorn and helped create what the company calls the sleep fitness movement. Eight Sleep now sells in 37 countries. She’s expecting her first child in January with her husband, Matteo, the company’s co-founder and CEO.

Sources indicate that alexandra Zatarain: So many things. I just turned 37, and I’ve seen so many friends go through pregnancy before me. After my first trimester, I felt so bad, thinking, what a terrible friend I was. When you haven’t experienced it, you have such little empathy for what a woman’s body is going through, especially when life keeps demanding so much of you and it doesn’t stop. I really didn’t understand that you could feel so different in your body for so long. It’s built so much more admiration for women and what we go through, and it’s let me embrace a feminine side of myself that in tech you usually don’t get to bring out.

Alexandra Zatarain: It’s made me realize that the only way the world out there is going to change for our benefit as women and mothers is if more of us are the ones making the decisions. I just don’t see any way around it. We have a lot of parents at Eight Sleep, every executive on our team is a parent, but as a woman the experience is completely different. Unless we can share that first-hand knowledge, it’s going to be hard to make progress as fast as we need to. It’s unfortunate that it takes the first-person experience to become that advocate, because everyone should appreciate what mothers go through, given that we all come from a mother.

Alexandra Zatarain: A couple of years ago, our clinical team, which is more than 90% women, was analyzing data from our user base and noticed our technology had been improving men’s sleep more than women’s. They asked, what are we missing in how we design this? It turned out the algorithms that manage temperature while you sleep had been fed more data representing men than women. That’s a classic problem in science, where women are underrepresented because our bodies are more complex. You have to account for where someone is in their hormonal journey, pregnancy, postpartum, perimenopause. So we invested a couple million dollars into research and developed features from it. That changed how we think about ourselves, less about helping everyone in a broad way and more about solving specific problems women have had for ages.

Recent findings suggest that alexandra Zatarain: Sleep is the most notable pillar of health. You would die sooner from sleep deprivation than from food deprivation, which tells you how fundamental it is. For women it matters even more because our hormones rule our lives, and sleep is the one tool we have to regulate them. If you sleep well, your chances of better hormonal balance go up significantly. It’s the best medicine we have, more than working out, more than any meal. The challenge is that those same hormones are often playing against us, making it harder to sleep well in different seasons of life, so keeping our routines as stable as possible helps counter what our bodies are going through.

Alexandra Zatarain: The mindset piece is really important. There’s so much going on, the anxiety, the intrusive thoughts, so not being too hard on yourself is the first step. Understanding that the season will pass should put you a little more at ease, because it’s not going to be your life forever. The other piece is setting yourself up with the right systems, and the most important one is available to everyone for free, which is routine. It helps your body a lot. When you do need to sleep, it’ll be easier for your body to fall asleep because it’s used to the schedule.

Recent findings suggest that alexandra Zatarain: I’m very rigid about my sleep schedule. I travel a lot, so sleep is number one for me. I make space for eight to nine hours every night, and I’m pretty good at hitting it. I go to bed by 9:30 or 10 every single night no matter where I am in the world, and I don’t really use an alarm unless I have to wake up before 6, because my body just wakes up on its own. That schedule is the thing that’s changed my life the most. Second to that is the environment, the temperature in my room and my bed, the lights going dark, no noise.

It has been revealed that alexandra Zatarain: I think of myself as an athlete, and we’re all sort of athletes in a way. My sport is making decisions about how to build this business, and that means I have to train, stay healthy and think long term. It’s not a sprint. We’ve been doing this for 12 years, so the question is how do I not burn out and stay here 20 or 30 years more. I’m also lucky I built this with my husband, so there’s no real line between business and personal life for us. It’s all mixed in, but it’s so purpose-driven that achieving that purpose every day is what feeds the energy.

According to recent reports, alexandra Zatarain: I’m very open with them about how intentional I was. I did my embryo freezing in my early 30s because of where I was in life. And I tell them that if they want a career after they have a family, the best time to build equity in that career is to push as hard as you can before. Know what you want, because time isn’t always on our side as women. Move up the ranks, so that by the time you have kids you have more flexibility and maybe a higher income. It is possible, but it takes planning, it will require compromises, and very importantly it will require the right partner.

Alexandra Zatarain: It starts with the people around you understanding what you truly need. Sometimes it’s as simple as the encouragement of, yes, go take a nap, yes, your body’s going through a lot. It gets harder once the baby’s home and the mom is maybe exclusively breastfeeding, because it really all falls on you. So have a proposal in place ahead of time for how the load is going to be shared. Our partners are much more involved than previous generations, so have those conversations early. It doesn’t end with the birth plan. That’s where everything starts.

Industry observers note that alexandra Zatarain: The first trimester was difficult, a lot of nausea, and it was very hard to function at the level I’m used to. I almost never get sick, so feeling sick every day was a huge shift. It put me in the trajectory to build the team that would make it possible for me to become a mother, to figure out what to delegate and who to elevate, and I’ve built a stronger team as a result. But the biggest thing is that it’s taught me to let go. I can’t control how I feel every day. As a Type A person I always want to be in control, and this has been like therapy, learning that I’m not in control of my body. I’m building a human, and it’s fine if for this season things just work differently.

  • What’s great is that you can buy a lot more with it than just your basic bandages or the odd bottle of contact solution.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bonus: They’re all literally proven to be good for you, too!

In a recent development, here’s a fun fact about your Flexible Spending Account (FSA): whatever you don’t spend by the deadline is gone. Granted, some intends give you a little grace period or rollover a small amount, but most of us are on the use-it-or-lose-it clock. And while Health Savings Account (HSA) money doesn’t expire, it’s still sitting there earmarked for your health, and the holidays are a good excuse to finally use it.

What’s great is that you can buy a lot more with it than just your basic bandages or the odd bottle of contact solution. We’re talking heating pads, period underwear, sunscreen, smart rings... even ergonomic office chairs can qualify! Some of the bigger-ticket items here (like the Lettuce Grow) may require a letter of medical necessity, but that typically just means filling out a quick online health questionnaire at checkout through a service like Truemed or Flex. Everything else you can usually just swipe your HSA/FSA card for. Of course, rules vary by strategy, so check yours if you’re not sure.

Industry observers note that one notable caveat: HSA/FSA funds can only be used for you, your spouse, and your dependents. That means the following picks are perfect for treating yourself, stuffing your kids’ stockings, or, you know, finally getting your snoring partner something that’ll ultimately help you both sleep.

Here are some of our favorite items that are often covered by HSA and FSA guidelines.

It has been revealed that if you know someone who gets painful period cramps or has endometriosis or adenomyosis, these little menstrual heat pads are such a thoughtful stocking stuffer. I stick them inside the waistband of my pants, and it genuinely gets hot enough to offer relief and go wherever I go all day. They last for hours, and I just love that they let me get relief without feeling stuck to a heating pad (and therefore a wall outlet). — Katie McPherson.

Sources indicate that isn’t it great when really trendy, great-smelling, cute beauty products are also good for you and eligible to buy with tax-exempt money? This is the case with Touchland hand sanitizer, which is all the rage with tweens and teens, and for good reason. It’s so cute and fun that it makes keeping germs away a blast. This is so perfect for stocking stuffing. — Sarah Aswell.

As someone who works from home, I’ve always struggled with back pain from sitting hunched over a laptop all day long. I never even thought to check whether an office chair could be HSA/FSA-eligible... until I found out about Branch, which is usually through Truemed. Yes, you typically need to fill out a short form to get a letter of medical necessity, but it’s so worth it if the end result is a beautiful Branch office chair with 14 points of adjustment, including lumbar support that moves up, down, in and out, with armrests that adjust five ways. It’s also nice that there are so many upholstery options (I ordered the black boucle!). — Julie Sprankles.

Ancestry DNA Origins & Traits Kit.

While not all DNA kits are eligible for HSA and FSA spending accounts, ones that give you health information are usually kosher. This one, from Ancestry, falls into that category. Have fun learning more about yourself and your past while also finding out medical information that could change your life. This is a great gift for someone who has everything. — Sarah Aswell.

One of the most popular purchases with FSA and HSA money is this heated massage gun. It feels amazing, and it makes you feel better in the long run. We like this one because it gets killer reviews and comes with an app. Again, this is a big-ticket item that might turn out to be a great way to spend FSA money at the end of the year. — Sarah Aswell.

Industry observers note that I have a chronic illness that causes high inflammation, so I tend to have a lot of body pain... especially in my joints. This flexible, wearable device combines red light, infrared light, micro-vibration, and micro-magnetic pulses in one band. I’ve found that if I strap it on to whatever aches, it really seems to help ease the pain. You should be able to pay directly with your HSA/FSA card, but it’s always a good idea to check with your specific health blueprint to see if you need a letter of medical necessity. — Julie Sprankles.

Supergoop is one of my favorite beauty products and by far my favorite sunscreen tech giant. They make my skin look and feel great while protecting it for the future. Many of Supergoop’s products are FSA- and HSA-eligible, including this mineral eye cream that works like a dream. But don’t sleep on many of their other products — I also love their Unseen Sunscreen for faces. — Sarah Aswell.

Geniani XL Electric Heating Pad Throw.

I am not exaggerating when I say that my life was changed by breaking down and getting an electric heating pad for my bed. It makes my sore body feel better, it prevents stiffness, and it is also just really, really nice when I have my period and I’m feeling crampy. — Sarah Aswell.

This smart scale tracks 16 metrics, including muscle mass, body fat, and heart rate. You can pick the ones you want to show on the big color display and hide the rest, and it recognizes up to eight users. Plus, it syncs up with Apple Health and Google Health. Oh, and it has a few fun extra modes: Baby Mode (in case you need to check before your next pediatrician visit), Pet Mode (if your pup is on a diet), and Luggage Mode (so you know before heading to the airport). — Julie Sprankles.

I’m not proud of it, but in my middle age I’ve become a pretty bad snorer. The best gift I’ve ever gotten for my partner is these Ozlo earbuds, which can’t be beat. They are really comfortable to sleep in, and the white noise makes you catch your Zs like a baby. The price is a bit splurgy, but can you put a dollar sign on deep sleep, especially if you can put it on your HSA card? — Sarah Aswell.

VisoOne Blue Light Blocking Glasses.

Recent findings suggest that man, do some reading about blue light glasses, and you’ll see that they have virtually no downside — especially if you wear them at night while looking at screens. It’s probably the best thing you can buy for yourself under $20 that can help you feel better and get better sleep. And VisoOne has some really cute styles, too. — Sarah Aswell.

In a recent development, I’ve always wanted an Oura ring but held off because (a) I’m a mom and tend to buy everything for everyone else first and (b) this is more than I normally spend on myself. So I was pleasantly surprised to find out it’s HSA/FSA-eligible! The Oura Ring 4 looks like regular jewelry but tracks more than 50 metrics like sleep, stress, heart health, cycle, and more, which is hugely helpful always but especially when you’re in perimenopause like so many of us on the Scary Mommy team are. — Julie Sprankles.

Keep Going Travel Family First Aid Kit.

In a recent development, I love giving first-aid kits to people for the holidays, especially if someone has recently gotten a newly introduced car, moved into a new place, or had a new baby. We should really have more of these in more places — and my favorite one is this cute portable one by Keep Going. There are so many cute patterns, and it fits anywhere from your glove box to a tote to a diaper bag. — Sarah Aswell.

Saalt Hanky Panky Boy Short Period Underwear.

I love period undies so much! They don’t leak, they’re good for the environment, and they will save you a significant amount of money over time. My favorite pair is these boy shorts from Saalt called Hanky Panky. They have great coverage while also still managing to be cute. Most, if not all, period panties are eligible to be purchased with your HSA or FSA! — Sarah Aswell.

Caring Mill Vapor Shower Tablets.

Sources indicate that one of my favorite discoveries of 2025 was shower tablets — also known as shower steamers. You throw them onto the floor of the shower and, over the course of your rinse, they evaporate and let off fumes infused with essential oils. Certain types can help clear out your sinuses (peppermint) or relax you for bed (lavender). They’re fun and they have a purpose. I like these from Caring Mill, which is a brand specifically for people buying HSA and FSA items. — Sarah Aswell.

Neutrogena Pink Grapefruit Cleansing Wipes.

In a recent development, these cleansing wipes are great for everything from removing grit and makeup at night to keeping in your purse for a little refresh during the day. And they smell divine! — Sarah Aswell.

I’ve had my Lettuce Grow for over a year now, and it’s one of my most favorite things in our house! It’s like having your own personal salad bar. The Nook grows 20 plants under built-in grow lights, and they arrive pre-sprouted, so you’re harvesting about twice as fast as you would from seed. It's such a great option for families who want to get more greens on the table, and it’s HSA/FSA-eligible through Flex. — Julie Sprankles.

In a recent development, I’ve been putting pimple patches in my daughters’ holiday stockings for a few years now, but only recently have I tried them out and discovered that they actually work and are really awesome! Many of them qualify for HSA/FSA purchases, especially if they are medicated. I love these spot patches from Curology, which contain the active ingredient hydrocolloid. — Sarah Aswell.

Cure Hydrating Electrolyte Drink Mix.

I was surprised to find that some hydration drink mixes are FSA- and HSA-approved. Which is great because sometimes when I’m feeling rundown, I just put one of these in a significant glass of water and feel so much better. — Sarah Aswell.

#101901. Menopause Is Hurting Women at Work. Something Has To Change.

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (914 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scarymommy ↗ Open Full Page

Menopause Is Hurting Women at Work. Something Has To Change.

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (914 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here’s what women can actually do about it.
  • I distinctly remember sitting in AP English class as a junior in high school with such horrible period cramps that it must've shown on my face.
  • It was the first time in my life that I hadn’t felt well and advocated for myself, albeit only after being nudged.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Brain fog, hot flashes, no sleep... and zero workplace support. Here’s what women can actually do about it.

I distinctly remember sitting in AP English class as a junior in high school with such horrible period cramps that it must've shown on my face. I kept staring at the clock, and eventually, my very strict, no-nonsense teacher came to my desk and asked if I was OK.

“Can I go home early?” I asked.

It was the first time in my life that I hadn’t felt well and advocated for myself, albeit only after being nudged.

In a recent development, then, in my 20s, I was severely nauseous with my first pregnancy but kept suffering through it at work because I wanted to save up my PTO for maternity leave. Now, I work from home, but as I’m hitting my late 30s, I wonder if I’d be any better at advocating for my needs in the workplace if I had perimenopause symptoms.

Recent findings suggest that truthfully, I’m not sure I would be — and I’m far from the only one. In a fresh study, Womea surveyed more than 830 employed U.S. women ages 45 and older about how perimenopause or menopause symptoms affect their experiences at work.

It has been revealed that of those surveyed, 60% noted no one at work knew they were experiencing symptoms. Meanwhile, 90% said their employers have no menopause or midlife health policies in place. An alarming 87% said their symptoms affected their job performance in the past year, and 17% believed their symptoms cost them a promotion, raise, or high-visibility project.

So what’s a woman to do when she finds her perimenopause or menopause symptoms interfering with her career? And what can we reasonably expect our employers to do about it?

Recent findings suggest that perimenopause is the hormonal transition that leads us on the lovely path to menopause. It can begin in a woman’s 30s, although it more commonly starts in her 40s. “Fun” symptoms include brain fog, sleep disruption, mood changes, hot flashes, and irregular periods.

Dr. Gillian Goddard, a board-certified endocrinologist and author of The Hormone Loop, states disrupted sleep can leave a woman feeling physically and mentally sluggish. Declining estrogen levels also affect dopamine activity, making it harder to concentrate. Research also suggests that learning latest information can become more difficult during this period.

That helps explain why half of the women in the Womea survey reported experiencing brain fog or losing their train of thought during a meeting, client call, or presentation.

Women in this stage might not feel like themselves physically and emotionally, indicates Lauren Tetenbaum, LCSW, JD, PMH-C, MSCP, a Upcoming York-based women’s reproductive mental health expert and the author of Millennial Menopause: Preparing for Perimenopause, Menopause, and Life’s Next Period.

As a psychotherapist, Tetenbaum says many of her clients are ambitious and dedicated to their careers, but are “caught off guard by the symptoms… they were never warned about.” Not even by their own healthcare providers!

According to recent reports, rather than recognizing that they may need medical care or additional rest, some women catastrophize what they’re going through, she says, worrying that brain fog could be a sign of early dementia or that they’re no longer capable of meeting their own high standards. “The performance is often not the matter; it’s the self-perception,” Tetenbaum says.

Still, it’s not easy for women navigating midlife at work.

Women can feel pushed out of the workforce during major life transitions, Tetenbaum notes, from matrescence to perimenopause, because they're presented with a false choice: “Sacrifice your health or wellbeing or values to work here, or leave, and don’t you dare show ‘weakness’ by asking for help.”.

We shouldn’t have to choose between our health and our careers... nor should we feel obligated to disclose personal medical details to our managers just to get support.

It has been revealed that instead, Tetenbaum encourages women to familiarize themselves with their workplace benefits, such as health insurance coverage, PTO, and possible accommodations. (Sometimes, especially in competitive fields, employees can worry that taking PTO makes them look noncommitted. But taking care of ourselves shouldn't be seen as professional weakness. After all, we can’t bring our best selves to work if we're not feeling our best.).

Tetenbaum also strongly urges women to seek medical care rather than assume they have to push through their symptoms.

Employers have to do their part, too.

Sources indicate that goddard states several workplace conditions can make this phase of life more difficult for women, including insufficient restrooms, unpredictable or long hours, limited opportunities for breaks, and confined workspaces. Addressing some of these conditions could make a difference.

Employers can also review their health insurance policies to make sure menopause-related care is covered, such as menopause specialists, behavioral and psychological health care, and other relevant services, adds Tetenbaum, as well as look at ways to implement flexible schedules, remote work options, temperature controls, and uniforms that don’t exacerbate symptoms.

Of course, every individual and workplace is different. So employers should never be afraid to ask employees what would help them, she claims.

As for women thinking about leaving their jobs or reducing their hours because of symptoms, Tetenbaum cautions, “Try not to make long-term decisions during a moment you feel overwhelmed.”.

In a recent development, and the best decision we can make of all? Learning to advocate for our needs... in every stage of our careers and bodies.

#101900. Breaking: Your kid needs you to have hobbies outside of motherhood. Here’s why

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (903 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Mother ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Your kid needs you to have hobbies outside of motherhood. Here’s why

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (903 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mother

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that twenty-four years.
  • Sources indicate that A whistle blew.
  • Recent findings suggest that when I got out of the pool, I walked over to my kids.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that twenty-four years. That’s how long it had been since I last stood atop a swim block, preparing to dive in for a timed race in an official meet.

Sources indicate that A whistle blew. The crowd hushed to silence. A monotone call came over the loudspeaker, “Swimmers, take your mark,” followed by a loud electronic beep that signaled the start of the race. I felt the cold rush of water overtake my body upon diving in. The neurons in my brain feverishly told my muscles to complete the strokes I’d learned decades before. In seconds, it was done. I finished the race.

Recent findings suggest that when I got out of the pool, I walked over to my kids. My son, a competitive swimmer himself, looked at me and earnestly stated, “Wow, Mom. I’m proud of you.”.

Recent findings suggest that like most moms, I have a packed schedule. I work, parent, volunteer at school, shepherd my two kids to practices and social gatherings, throw meals together, walk the dog, and occasionally find a moment to breathe. But over the past couple of years, I watched my growing kids, now ages 12 and 9, discover and engage in passions that light them up. It left me wondering, why not me, too?

In a recent development, “A recurring theme in my practice is women feeling they’ve lost their individual identities somewhere between work, parenting, and meeting everyone else’s needs,” says Carly Snyder, a Newly introduced York City–based reproductive and perinatal psychiatrist. “Part of my work involves helping women recognize that their own interests and needs are legitimate.”.

Research highlights a multitude of benefits earned by pursuing hobbies. Hobbyists often have wider social networks, improved mental health markers, and enhanced positive emotions.

Hobbies offer a particularly important lifeline for mothers, who often report losing themselves to the demanding needs of family life. That rings true for Kaitlyn Edington, an art educator and mom of two who recalls struggling after returning to work as a teacher following the birth of her first child. “I was so depleted,” Edington notes. She spent her workdays teaching with short breaks to pump, often bringing her computer into her pumping room so she could catch up on work, then went home to full nights of infant care.

One day while scrolling on Instagram, Edington saw an artist posting images of her sketchbook paintings. “She changed my life,” Edington states. “Her sketchbook paintings were so loose and free, and she was encouraging people to draw everyday. I remember thinking, ‘If I have to pump two to three times a day, which I absolutely hate, why not pair it with something that I love?’” From then on, Edington sketched when she pumped, and ultimately developed a habit of daily sketching that she continues 10 years later.

No longer in the pumping phase of life, Edington ensures she gets time to sketch by waking up before her kids. “I hold the habit of waking up before my kids as sacred,” she says. “I need that time, when nobody needs me. It’s my emotional rest.”.

Science backs Edington’s belief that her hobby stabilizes her mental health. “Reengaging in meaningful, enjoyable activities can be therapeutically valuable,” Snyder indicates. “Behavioral activation, an evidence-based treatment for depression, specifically emphasizes reconnecting with activities that provide pleasure, purpose, or a sense of accomplishment.”.

Snyder has three children, ages 19, 16, and 11, and throughout their lives she has maintained her dedication to skiing, cycling, yoga and running, completing a total of 19 marathons. She knows her kids benefit from her hobbies. Each time Snyder trains for an upcoming marathon, “[My kids] witness my commitment, discipline, setbacks, and perseverance,” she notes. “Watching a parent pursue a hobby provides opportunities to observe persistence, emotional regulation, problem-solving, and enjoyment.”.

But those benefits are secondary to the impacts hobbies have on the women pursuing them. “I think we’ve become so accustomed to framing everything mothers do in terms of how it benefits their children,” Snyder notes. “Women are entitled to happiness and fulfillment for their own sake.”.

It’s simply an added bonus that when mom is happy for mom’s sake, the benefits for her kids naturally follow, according to multiple studies linking a mother’s well-being with her child’s. Plus, kids also learn that all stages of adulthood, including those under the umbrella of parenting, can include personal fulfillment, curiosity, and growth.

The best way to start a hobby is to let yourself reconnect with something you already love. I remembered how much joy I got out of competing in swim meets in high school, and I was eager to recreate that glee. Ask yourself, “What did I love when I was a kid or a young adult?”.

Your hobby doesn’t have to involve intense commitment. “Reading, gardening, dancing, listening to music, or simply spending time alone can be just as meaningful as running a marathon,” Snyder notes.

Search online for local groups involved in the activity you want to pursue. Your local library may have resources to help you get started as well.

Sources indicate that when you’re ready to commit, set realistic goals. Start by focusing on your hobby consistently for just 10-15 minutes per day. Showing up is the main goal.

According to recent reports, “Motherhood should expand a woman’s identity, not erase it,” Snyder advises. Which hobby will help expand yours?

As the story of Gelatoâs unusual mode of transport spread, drawing plenty of social media attention, it also caught the eye of Hope Hollandsworth, a 28-year-old tattoo artist and devoted cat parent. When she first saw a photograph of Gelato during the summer, she felt immediately drawn to him.

Absolutely. A disability does not automatically mean that a cat has a poor quality of life. Cats with mobility challenges can still enjoy affection, play, exploration, food puzzles, comfortable naps, and the organization of people they trust.

What really matters is understanding the individual cat's needs and making reasonable adjustments to help them live comfortably.

For a cat with a spinal injury, this may include providing easy access to food, water, resting areas, and litter boxes. Non-slip flooring, ramps, and thoughtfully arranged furniture can also help some cats move around more safely. Sources indicate that toddlers are a wild ride. They’re old enough to have opinions, verbal enough to pepper in words like “actually” and small enough to go fully boneless in the cereal aisle when overruled. But with the right frame of mind and a little patience, we can outsmart them.

(If you try this one, stick with a foil balloon, since popped latex is a choking hazard for little kids.).

Brushing teeth, putting on shoes, surviving the checkout aisle. The daily stuff is where most battles originate, and, in turn, where moms get the most inventive. A common thread here is giving toddlers a sense of control while you cleverly steer the ship.

Credit: @parentnest.digital via Threads.

Credit: @suziespree via Threads.

And sometimes the smartest move is picking your battles.

From there, a little misdirection can work wonders.

And for the moments when you’re the one about to lose it, one mom has a suggestion that sounds unhinged until you hear her out.
